title: Activepieces Integrations List for 2026, by Category
summary: The Activepieces integrations list shows available connectors. Verify your app's required triggers and actions are supported before committing.
body_markdown:
## Integration coverage costs


Every automation platform faces the same problem: each app has its own API, authentication scheme and quirks, and someone has to write and maintain an adapter for each one. A connector is that adapter, and the cost of building them grows with every app added.


Triggers are the expensive part. An app that pushes events through webhooks lets a platform react instantly, while one that doesn't forces the platform to poll on a schedule, compare results with the last run and work out what is new.


**Many connectors ship with actions only** , because actions are far easier to build than reliable triggers.


### Polling, webhooks and the work behind a trigger


A polling trigger asks the app on a timer, often every few minutes, and keeps a record of what it saw last time so it passes on only new items. A webhook trigger registers a URL with the app and waits to be called.


Webhooks are faster and cheaper, but the app has to offer them, and the connector has to re-register them when they lapse.


Authentication adds its own load. OAuth tokens expire and need refreshing, API keys need safe storage, and rate limits can throttle a busy flow. Pagination quirks and renamed fields quietly break connectors that nobody tests.


### How platforms expand their integration catalogs


Vendors have settled on a handful of approaches. Some staff a team to build and certify connectors in-house, which gives consistent quality but follows the vendor's roadmap. Some open the catalog to community contributors, which grows breadth faster and varies in depth.


Others generate connectors from an app's OpenAPI description, which is quick but covers only what the spec describes. A fourth group puts a unified API in front of a whole category such as CRMs, trading app-specific fields for a single integration.


None of these removes the long tail, so nearly every platform also ships a generic HTTP step and a code step. They let you call an API the catalog never covered, at the price of handling authentication, pagination and error cases yourself.


Connectors also drift. An app changes a field name or retires an API version, and a connector that worked last quarter starts failing.


Vendors with their own teams patch this centrally, while community catalogs depend on someone noticing, so check when an integration was last touched.


### How to evaluate an integrations catalog


Whichever approach a platform takes, the useful test is the same. List the events and actions your workflows need, then check each against the connector itself. An app count, whoever publishes it, says how many adapters exist, not how deep any one of them goes.
